  "passage_text": "THE LEGEND OF HORUS OF BEHUTET AND THE WINGED DISK

The text of this Legend is cut in hieroglyphs on the walls of the temple
of Edfu, in Upper Egypt, and some of the incidents described in it are
illustrated by large bas-reliefs. The form of the Legend here given
dates from the Ptolemaic Period, but the subject matter is some
thousands of years older. The great historical fact underlying the
Legend is the Conquest of Egypt by some very early king who invaded
Egypt from the south, and who succeeded in conquering every part of it,
even the northern part of the Delta. The events described are supposed
to have taken place whilst Ra was still reigning on the earth. The
Legend states that in the three hundred and sixty-third year of the
reign of Ra-Harmakhis, the ever living, His Majesty was in Ta-sti
(_i.e._ the Land of the Bow, or Nubia) with his soldiers; the enemy had
reviled him, and for this reason the land is called "Uauatet" to this
day. From Nubia Ra sailed down the river to Apollinopolis (Edfu), and
Heru-Behutet, or Horus of Edfu, was with him. On arriving there Horus
told Ra that the enemy were plotting against him, and Ra told him to go
out and slay them. Horus took the form of a great winged disk, which
flew up into the air and pursued the enemy, and it attacked them with
such terrific force that they could neither see nor hear, and they fell
upon each other, and slew each other, and in a moment not a single foe
was left alive. Then Horus returned to the Boat of Ra-Harmakhis, in the
form of the winged disk which shone with many colours, and said,
"Advance, O Ra, and look upon thine enemies who are lying under thee in
this land." Ra set out on the journey, taking with him the goddess
Ashtoreth, and he saw his enemies lying on the ground, each of them
being fettered. After looking upon his slaughtered foes Ra said to the
gods who were with him, "Behold, let us sail in our boat on the water,
for our hearts are glad because our enemies have been overthrown on the
earth." So the Boat of Ra moved onwards towards the north, and the
enemies of the god who were on the banks took the form of crocodiles and
hippopotami, and tried to frighten the god, for as his boat came near
them they opened their jaws wide, intending to swallow it up together
with the gods who were in it. Among the crew were the Followers of Horus
of Edfu, who were skilled workers in metal, and each of these had in his
hands an iron spear and a chain. These "Blacksmiths" threw out their
chains into the river and allowed the crocodiles and hippopotami to
entangle their legs in them, and then they dragged the beasts towards
the bows of the Boat, and driving their spears into their bodies, slew
them there. After the slaughter the bodies of six hundred and fifty-one
crocodiles were brought and laid out before the town of Edfu. When Thoth
saw these he said, "Let your hearts rejoice, O gods of heaven, Let your
hearts rejoice, O ye gods who dwell on the earth. The Young Horus cometh
in peace. On his way he hath made manifest deeds of valour, according to
the Book of slaying the Hippopotamus." And from that day they made
figures of Horus in metal.

Then Horus of Edfu took the form of the winged disk, and set himself on
the prow of the Boat of Ra. He took with him Nekhebet, goddess of the
South, and Uatchet, goddess of the North, in the form of serpents, so
that they might make all the enemies of the Sun-god to quake in the
South and in the North. His foes who had fled to the north doubled back
towards the south, for they were in deadly fear of the god. Horus
pursued and overtook them, and he and his blacksmiths had in their hands
spears and chains, and they slew large numbers of them to the south-east
of the town of Thebes in Upper Egypt. Many succeeded in escaping towards
the north once more, but after pursuing them for a whole day Horus
overtook them, and made a great slaughter among them. Meanwhile the
other foes of the god, who had heard of the defeats of their allies,
fled into Lower Egypt, and took refuge among the swamps of the Delta.
Horus set out after them, and came up with them, and spent four days in
the water slaying his foes, who tried to escape in the forms of
crocodiles and hippopotami. He captured one hundred and forty-two of the
enemy and a male hippopotamus, and took them to the fore part of the
Boat of Ra. There he hacked them in pieces, and gave their inward parts
to his followers, and their mutilated bodies to the gods and goddesses
who were in the Boat of Ra and on the river banks in the town of Heben.

Then the remnant of the enemy turned their faces towards the Lake of the
North, and they attempted to sail to the Mediterranean in boats; but the
terror of Horus filled their hearts, and they left their boats and fled
to the district of Mertet-Ament, where they joined themselves to the
worshippers of Set, the god of evil, who dwelt in the Western Delta.
Horus pursued them in his boat for one day and one night without seeing
them, and he arrived at the town of Per-Rehui. At length he discovered
the position of the enemy, and he and his followers fell upon them, and
slew a large number of them; he captured three hundred and eighty-one of
them alive, and these he took to the Boat of Ra, then, having slain
them, he gave their carcases to his followers or bodyguard, who
presumably devoured them. The custom of eating the bodies of enemies is
very old in Egypt, and survives in some parts of Africa to this day."
}

  "passage_text": "Then Set, the great antagonist of Horus, came out and cursed him for the
slaughter of his people, using most shameful words of abuse. Horus stood
up and fought a duel with Set, the "Stinking Face," as the text calls
him, and Horus succeeded in throwing him to the ground and spearing him.
Horus smashed his mouth with a blow of his mace, and having fettered him
with his chain, he brought him into the presence of Ra, who ordered that
he was to be handed over to Isis and her son Horus, that they might work
their will on him. Here we must note that the ancient editor of the
Legend has confounded Horus the ancient Sun-god with Horus, son of Isis,
son of Osiris. Then Horus, the son of Isis, cut off the heads of Set and
his followers in the presence of Ra, and dragged Set by his feet round
about throughout the district with his spear driven through his head and
back, according to the order of Ra. The form which Horus of Edfu had at
that time was that of a man of great strength, with the face and back of
a hawk; on his head he wore the Double Crown, with feathers and serpents
attached, and in his hands he held a metal spear and a metal chain. And
Horus, the son of Isis, took upon himself a similar form, and the two
Horuses slew all the enemies on the bank of the river to the west of the
town of Per-Rehui. This slaughter took place on the seventh day of the
first month of the season Pert,[1] which was ever afterwards called the
"Day of the Festival of Sailing."

[Footnote 1: About the middle of November.]

Now, although Set in the form of a man had been slain, he reappeared in
the form of a great hissing serpent, and took up his abode in a hole in
the ground without being noticed by Horus. Ra, however, saw him, and
gave orders that Horus, the son of Isis, in the form of a hawk-headed
staff, should set himself at the mouth of the hole, so that the monster
might never reappear among men. This Horus did, and Isis his mother
lived there with him. Once again it became known to Ra that a remnant of
the followers of Set had escaped, and that under the direction of the
Smait fiends, and of Set, who had reappeared, they were hiding in the
swamps of the Eastern Delta. Horus of Edfu, the winged disk, pursued
them, speared them, and finally slew them in the presence of Ra. For the
moment there were no more enemies of Ra to be found in the district on
land, although Horus passed six days and six nights in looking for them;
but it seems that several of the followers of Set in the forms of water
reptiles were lying on the ground under water, and that Horus saw them
there. At this time Horus had strict guard kept over the tomb of Osiris
in Anrutef,[1] because he learned that the Smait fiends wanted to come
and wreck both it and the body of the god. Isis, too, never ceased to
recite spells and incantations in order to keep away her husband's foes
from his body. Meanwhile the "blacksmiths" of Horus, who were in charge
of the "middle regions" of Egypt, found a body of the enemy, and
attacked them fiercely, slew many of them, and took one hundred and six
of them prisoners. The "blacksmiths" of the west also took one hundred
and six prisoners, and both groups of prisoners were slain before Ra. In
return for their services Ra bestowed dwelling-places upon the
"blacksmiths," and allowed them to have temples with images of their
gods in them, and arranged for offerings and libations to be made to
them by properly appointed priests of various classes.

[Footnote 1: A district of Herakleopolis.]

Shortly after these events Ra discovered that a number of his enemies
were still at large, and that they had sailed in boats to the swamps
that lay round about the town of Tchal, or Tchar, better known as Zoan
or Tanis. Once more Horus unmoored the Boat of Ra, and set out against
them; some took refuge in the waters, and others landed and escaped to
the hilly land on the east. For some reason, which is not quite
apparent, Horus took the form of a mighty lion with a man's face, and he
wore on his head the triple crown. His claws were like flints, and he
pursued the enemy on the hills, and chased them hither and thither, and
captured one hundred and forty-two of them. He tore out their tongues,
and ripped their bodies into strips with his claws, and gave them over
to his allies in the mountains, who, no doubt, ate them. This was the
last fight in the north of Egypt, and Ra proposed that they should sail
up the river and return to the south. They had traversed all Egypt, and
sailed over the lakes in the Delta, and down the arms of the Nile to the
Mediterranean, and as no more of the enemy were to be seen the prow of
the boat of Ra was turned southwards. Thoth recited the spells that
produced fair weather, and said the words of power that prevented storms
from rising, and in due course the Boat reached Nubia. When it arrived
Horus found in the country of Uauatet men who were conspiring against
him and cursing him, just as they had at one time blasphemed Ra. Horus,
taking the form of the winged disk, and accompanied by the two
serpent-goddesses, Nekhebet and Uatchet, attacked the rebels, but there
was no fierce fighting this time, for the hearts of the enemy melted
through fear of him. His foes cast themselves before him on the ground
in submission, they offered no resistance, and they died straightway.
Horus then returned to the town of Behutet (Edfu), and the gods
acclaimed him, and praised his prowess. Ra was so pleased with him that
he ordered Thoth to have a winged disk, with a serpent on each side of
it, placed in every temple in Egypt in which he (_i.e._ Ra) was
worshipped, so that it might act as a protector of the building, and
drive away any and every fiend and devil that might wish to attack it.
This is the reason why we find the winged disk, with a serpent on each
side of it, above the doors of temples and religious buildings
throughout the length and breadth of Egypt."

  "passage_text": "In many places in the text that contains the above Legend there are\nshort passages in which attempts are made to explain the origins of the\nnames of certain towns and gods. All these are interpolations in the\nnarrative made by scribes at a late period of Egyptian history. As it\nwould be quite useless to reproduce them without many explanatory notes,\nfor which there is no room in this little book, they have been omitted.\n\n            THE LEGEND OF KHNEMU AND A SEVEN YEARS' FAMINE\n\nThis Legend is cut in hieroglyphs on a large rounded block of granite,\nwhich stands on the south-east portion of Sahal, a little island in the\nFirst Cataract in Upper Egypt, two or three miles to the south of the\nmodern town of Aswan, the ancient Syene. The form of the Legend, and the\nshapes of the hieroglyphs, and the late spelling of the words, prove\nthat the inscription is the work of the Ptolemaic Period, though it is\npossible that the Legend in its simplest form is as old as the period to\nwhich it is ascribed in the Sahal text, namely, the third dynasty, about\n4100 B.C. The subject of the Legend is a terrible famine, which lasted\nfor seven years, in the reign of King Tcheser, and which recalls the\nseven years' famine that took place in Egypt when Joseph was there. This\nfamine was believed to have been caused by the king's neglect to worship\nproperly the god Khnemu, who was supposed to control the springs of the\nNile, which were asserted by the sages to be situated between two great\nrocks on the Island of Elephantine. The Legend sets forth that the\nViceroy of Nubia, in the reign of Tcheser, was a nobleman called Meter,\nwho was also the overseer of all the temple properties in the South. His\nresidence was in Abu, or Elephantine, and in the eighteenth year of his\nreign the king sent him a despatch in which it was written thus: \"This\nis to inform thee that misery hath laid hold upon me as I sit upon the\ngreat throne, and I grieve for those who dwell in the Great House.[1] My\nheart is grievously afflicted by reason of a very great calamity, which\nis due to the fact that the waters of the Nile have not risen to their\nproper height for seven years. Grain is exceedingly scarce, there are no\ngarden herbs and vegetables to be had at all, and everything which men\nuse for food hath come to an end. Every man robbeth his neighbour. The\npeople wish to walk about, but are unable to move. The baby waileth, the\nyoung man shuffleth along on his feet through weakness. The hearts of\nthe old men are broken down with despair, their legs give way under\nthem, they sink down exhausted on the ground, and they lay their hands\non their bellies [in pain]. The officials are powerless and have no\ncounsel to give, and when the public granaries, which ought to contain\nsupplies, are opened, there cometh forth from them nothing but wind.\nEverything is in a state of ruin. I go back in my mind to the time when\nI had an adviser, to the time of the gods, to the Ibis-god [Thoth], and\nto the chief Kher-heb priest Imhetep (Imouthis),[2] the son of Ptah of\nhis South Wall.[3] [Tell me, I pray thee], Where is the birthplace of\nthe Nile? What god or what goddess presideth over it? What kind of form\nhath the god? For it is he that maketh my revenue, and who filleth the\ngranaries with grain. I wish to go to [consult] the Chief of\nHet-Sekhmet,[4] whose beneficence strengtheneth all men in their works.\nI wish to go into the House of Life,[5] and to take the rolls of the\nbooks in my own hands, so that I may examine them [and find out these\nthings].\"\n\n[Footnote 1: An allusion to the royal title of Pharaoh, in Egyptian\nPER-AA, the \"Great House,\" in whom and by whom all the Egyptians were\nsupposed to live.]\n\n[Footnote 2: A famous priest and magician of Memphis, who was\nsubsequently deified.]\n\n[Footnote 3: A part of Memphis.]\n\n[Footnote 4: _i.e._ Hermopolis, the town of Thoth.]\n\n[Footnote 5: _i.e._ the library of the temple.]"
}

  "passage_text": "Having read the royal despatch the Viceroy Meter set out to go to the
king, and when he came to him he proceeded to instruct the king in the
matters about which he had asked questions. The text makes the king say:
"[Meter] gave me information about the rise of the Nile, and he told me
all that men had written concerning it; and he made clear to me all the
difficult passages [in the books], which my ancestors had consulted
hastily, and which had never before been explained to any king since the
time when Ra [reigned]. And he said to me: There is a town in the river
wherefrom the Nile maketh his appearance. 'Abu' was its name in the
beginning: it is the City of the Beginning, it is the Name of the City
of the Beginning. It reacheth to Uauatet, which is the first land [on
the south]. There is a long flight of steps there (a nilometer?), on
which Ra resteth when he determineth to prolong life to mankind. It is
called 'Netchemtchem ankh.' Here are the 'Two Qerti,'[1] which are the
two breasts wherefrom every good thing cometh. Here is the bed of the
Nile, here the Nile-god reneweth his youth, and here he sendeth out the
flood on the land. Here his waters rise to a height of twenty-eight
cubits; at Hermopolis (in the Delta) their height is seven cubits. Here
the Nile-god smiteth the ground with his sandals, and here he draweth
the bolts and throweth open the two doors through which the water
poureth forth. In this town the Nile-god dwelleth in the form of Shu,
and he keepeth the account of the products of all Egypt, in order to
give to each his due. Here are kept the cord for measuring land and the
register of the estates. Here the god liveth in a wooden house with a
door made of reeds, and branches of trees form the roof; its entrance is
to the south-east. Round about it are mountains of stone to which
quarrymen come with their tools when they want stone to build temples to
the gods, shrines for sacred animals, and pyramids for kings, or to make
statues. Here they offer sacrifices of all kinds in the sanctuary, and
here their sweet-smelling gifts are presented before the face of the god
Khnemu. In the quarries on the river bank is granite, which is called
the 'stone of Abu.' The names of its gods are: Sept (Sothis, the
dog-star), Anqet, Hep (the Nile-god), Shu, Keb, Nut, Osiris, Horus,
Isis, and Nephthys. Here are found precious stones (a list is given),
gold, silver, copper, iron, lapis-lazuli, emerald, crystal, ruby, &c.,
alabaster, mother-of-emerald, and seeds of plants that are used in
making incense. These were the things which I learned from Meter [the
Viceroy]."

[Footnote 1: The two caverns which contained the springs of the Nile.]

Having informed the king concerning the rise of the Nile and the other
matters mentioned in his despatch, Meter made arrangements for the king
to visit the temple of Khnemu in person. This he did, and the Legend
gives us the king's own description of his visit. He says: I entered the
temple, and the keepers of the rolls untied them and showed them to me.
I was purified by the sprinkling of holy water, and I passed through the
places that were prohibited to ordinary folk, and a great offering of
cakes, ale, geese, oxen, &c., was offered up on my behalf to the gods
and goddesses of Abu. Then I found the god [Khnemu] standing in front of
me, and I propitiated him with the offerings that I made unto him, and I
made prayer and supplication before him. Then he opened his eyes,[1] and
his heart inclined to me, and in a majestic manner he said unto me: "I
am Khnemu who fashioned thee. My two hands grasped thee and knitted
together thy body; I made thy members sound, and I gave thee thy heart.
Yet the stones have been lying under the ground for ages, and no man
hath worked them in order to build a god-house, to repair the [sacred]
buildings which are in ruins, or to make shrines for the gods of the
South and North, or to do what he ought to do for his lord, even though
I am the Lord [the Creator]. I am Nu, the self-created, the Great God,
who came into being in the beginning. [I am] Hep [the Nile-god] who
riseth at will to give health to him that worketh for me. I am the
Governor and Guide of all men, in all their periods, the Most Great, the
Father of the gods, Shu, the Great One, the Chief of the earth. The two
halves of heaven are my abode. The Nile is poured out in a stream by me,
and it goeth round about the tilled lands, and its embrace produceth
life for every one that breatheth, according to the extent of its
embrace.... I will make the Nile to rise for thee, and in no year shall
it fail, and it shall spread its water out and cover every land
satisfactorily. Plants, herbs, and trees shall bend beneath [the weight
of] their produce. The goddess Rennet (the Harvest goddess) shall be at
the head of everything, and every product shall increase a hundred
thousandfold, according to the cubit of the year.[2] The people shall be
filled, verily to their hearts' desire, yea, everyone. Want shall cease,
and the emptiness of the granaries shall come to an end. The Land of
Mera (_i.e._ Egypt) shall be one cultivated land, the districts shall
be yellow with crops of grain, and the grain shall be good. The
fertility of the land shall be according to the desire [of the
husbandman], and it shall be greater than it hath ever been before." At
the sound of the word "crops" the king awoke, and the courage that then
filled his heart was as great as his former despair had been.

  "passage_text": "THE LEGEND OF THE WANDERINGS OF ISIS

The god Osiris, as we have seen in the chapter on the Egyptian Religion
in the accompanying volume, lived and reigned at one time upon earth in
the form of a man. His twin-brother Set was jealous of his popularity,
and hated him to such a degree that he contrived a plan whereby he
succeeded in putting Osiris to death. Set then tried to usurp his
brother's kingdom and to make himself sole lord of Egypt, and, although
no text states it distinctly, it is clear that he seized his brother's
wife, Isis, and shut her up in his house. Isis was, however, under the
protection of the god Thoth, and she escaped with her unborn child, and
the following Legend describes the incidents that befell her, and the
death and revivification of Horus. It is cut in hieroglyphs upon a large
stone stele which was made for Ankh-Psemthek, a prophet of Nebun in the
reign of Nectanebus I, who reigned from 373 B.C. to 360 B.C. The stele
was dug up in 1828 at Alexandria, and was given to Prince Metternich by
Muhammad Ali Pasha; it is now commonly known as the "Metternich Stele."
The Legend is narrated by the goddess herself, who says:

I am Isis. I escaped from the dwelling wherein my brother Set placed me.
Thoth, the great god, the Prince of Truth in heaven and on earth, said
unto me: "Come, O goddess Isis [hearken thou], it is a good thing to
hearken, for he who is guided by another liveth. Hide thyself with thy
child, and these things shall happen unto him. His body shall grow and
flourish, and strength of every kind shall be in him. He shall sit upon
his father's throne, he shall avenge him, and he shall hold the exalted
position of 'Governor of the Two Lands.'" I left the house of Set in the
evening, and there accompanied me Seven Scorpions, that were to travel
with me, and sting with their stings on my behalf. Two of them, Tefen
and Befen, followed behind me, two of them, Mestet and Mestetef, went
one on each side of me, and three, Petet, Thetet, and Maatet, prepared
the way for me. I charged them very carefully and adjured them to make
no acquaintance with any one, to speak to none of the Red Fiends, to pay
no heed to a servant (?), and to keep their gaze towards the ground so
that they might show me the way. And their leader brought me to Pa-Sui,
the town of the Sacred Sandals,[1] at the head of the district of the
Papyrus Swamps. When I arrived at Teb I came to a quarter of the town
where women dwelt. And a certain woman of quality spied me as I was
journeying along the road, and she shut her door in my face, for she was
afraid because of the Seven Scorpions that were with me. Then they took
counsel concerning her, and they shot out their poison on the tail of
Tefen. As for me, a peasant woman called Taha opened her door, and I
went into the house of this humble woman. Then the scorpion Tefen
crawled in under the door of the woman Usert [who had shut it in my
face], and stung her son, and a fire broke out in it; there was no water
to put it out, but the sky sent down rain, though it was not the time of
rain. And the heart of Usert was sore within her, and she was very sad,
for she knew not whether her son would live or die; and she went through
the town shrieking for help, but none came out at the sound of her
voice. And I was sad for the child's sake, and I wished the innocent one
to live again. So I cried out to her, saying, Come to me! Come to me!
There is life in my mouth. I am a woman well known in her town. I can
destroy the devil of death by a spell which my father taught me. I am
his daughter, his beloved one.

[Footnote 1: These places were in the seventh nome of Lower Egypt
(Metelites).]

Then Isis laid her hands on the child and recited this spell:

"O poison of Tefent, come forth, fall on the ground; go no further. O
poison of Befent, come forth, fall on the ground. I am Isis, the
goddess, the mistress of words of power. I am a weaver of spells, I know
how to utter words so that they take effect. Hearken to me, O every
reptile that biteth (or stingeth), and fall on the ground. O poison of
Mestet, go no further. O poison of Mestetef, rise not up in his body. O
poison of Petet and Thetet, enter not his body. O poison of Maatet, fall
on the ground. Ascend not into heaven, I command you by the beloved of
Ra, the egg of the goose which appeareth from the sycamore. My words
indeed rule to the uttermost limit of the night. I speak to you, O
scorpions. I am alone and in sorrow, and our names will stink throughout
the nomes.... The child shall live! The poison shall die! For Ra liveth
and the poison dieth. Horus shall be saved through his mother Isis, and
he who is stricken shall likewise be saved." Meanwhile the fire in the
house of Usert was extinguished, and heaven was content with the
utterance of Isis. Then the lady Usert was filled with sorrow because
she had shut her door in the face of Isis, and she brought to the house
of the peasant woman gifts for the goddess, whom she had apparently not
recognised. The spells of the goddess produced, of course, the desired
effect on the poison, and we may assume that the life of the child was
restored to him. The second lot of gifts made to Isis represented his
mother's gratitude."

  "passage_text": "Exactly when and how Isis made her way to a hiding place cannot be said,\nbut she reached it in safety, and her son Horus was born there. The\nstory of the death of Horus she tells in the following words: \"I am\nIsis. I conceived a child, Horus, and I brought him forth in a cluster\nof papyrus plants (or, bulrushes). I rejoiced exceedingly, for in him I\nsaw one who would make answer for his father. I hid him, and I covered\nhim up carefully, being afraid of that foul one [Set], and then I went\nto the town of Am, where the people gave thanks for me because they knew\nI could cause them trouble. I passed the day in collecting food for the\nchild, and when I returned and took Horus into my arms, I found him,\nHorus, the beautiful one of gold, the boy, the child, lifeless! He had\nbedewed the ground with the water of his eye and with the foam of his\nlips. His body was motionless, his heart did not beat, and his muscles\nwere relaxed.\" Then Isis sent forth a bitter cry, and lamented loudly\nher misfortune, for now that Horus was dead she had none to protect her,\nor to take vengeance on Set. When the people heard her voice they went\nout to her, and they bewailed with her the greatness of her affliction.\nBut though all lamented on her behalf there was none who could bring\nback Horus to life. Then a \"woman who was well known in her town, a lady\nwho was the mistress of property in her own right,\" went out to Isis,\nand consoled her, and assured her that the child should live through his\nmother. And she said, \"A scorpion hath stung him, the reptile Aunab hath\nwounded him.\" Then Isis bent her face over the child to find out if he\nbreathed, and she examined the wound, and found that there was poison in\nit, and then taking him in her arms, \"she leaped about with him like a\nfish that is put upon hot coals,\" uttering loud cries of lamentation.\nDuring this outburst of grief the goddess Nephthys, her sister, arrived,\nand she too lamented and cried bitterly over her sister's loss; with\nher came the Scorpion-goddess Serqet. Nephthys at once advised Isis to\ncry out for help to Ra, for, said she, it is wholly impossible for the\nBoat of Ra to travel across the sky whilst Horus is lying dead. Then\nIsis cried out, and made supplication to the Boat of Millions of Years,\nand the Sun-god stopped the Boat. Out of it came down Thoth, who was\nprovided with powerful spells, and, going to Isis, he inquired\nconcerning her trouble. \"What is it, what is it, O Isis, thou goddess of\nspells, whose mouth hath skill to utter them with supreme effect? Surely\nno evil thing hath befallen Horus, for the Boat of Ra hath him under its\nprotection. I have come from the Boat of the Disk to heal Horus.\" Then\nThoth told Isis not to fear, but to put away all anxiety from her heart,\nfor he had come to heal her child, and he told her that Horus was fully\nprotected because he was the Dweller in his disk, and the firstborn son\nof heaven, and the Great Dwarf, and the Mighty Ram, and the Great Hawk,\nand the Holy Beetle, and the Hidden Body, and the Governor of the Other\nWorld, and the Holy Benu Bird, and by the spells of Isis and the names\nof Osiris and the weeping of his mother and brethren, and by his own\nname and heart. Turning towards the child Thoth began to recite his\nspells and said, \"Wake up, Horus! Thy protection is established. Make\nthou happy the heart of thy mother Isis. The words of Horus bind up\nhearts and he comforteth him that is in affliction. Let your hearts\nrejoice, O ye dwellers in the heavens. Horus who avenged his father\nshall make the poison to retreat. That which is in the mouth of Ra shall\ncirculate, and the tongue of the Great God shall overcome [opposition].\nThe Boat of Ra standeth still and moveth not, and the Disk (_i.e._ the\nSun-god) is in the place where it was yesterday to heal Horus for his\nmother Isis. Come to earth, draw nigh, O Boat of Ra, O ye mariners of\nRa; make the boat to move and convey food of the town of Sekhem (_i.e._\nLetopolis) hither, to heal Horus for his mother Isis.... Come to earth,\nO poison! I am Thoth, the firstborn son, the son of Ra. Tem and the\ncompany of the gods have commanded me to heal Horus for his mother Isis.\nO Horus, O Horus, thy Ka protecteth thee, and thy Image worketh\nprotection for thee. The poison is as the daughter of its own flame; it\nis destroyed because it smote the strong son. Your temples are safe, for\nHorus liveth for his mother.\" Then the child Horus returned to life, to\nthe great joy of his mother, and Thoth went back to the Boat of Millions\nof Years, which at once proceeded on its majestic course, and all the\ngods from one end of heaven to the other rejoiced. Isis entreated either\nRa or Thoth that Horus might be nursed and brought up by the goddesses\nof the town of Pe-Tep, or Buto, in the Delta, and at once Thoth\ncommitted the child to their care, and instructed them about his future.\nHorus grew up in Buto under their protection, and in due course fought a\nduel with Set, and vanquished him, and so avenged the wrong done to his\nfather by Set.\n\n                    THE LEGEND OF KHENSU-NEFER-HETEP\n                      AND THE PRINCESS OF BEKHTEN"

  "passage_text": "Here for convenience' sake may be inserted the story of the Possessed\nPrincess of Bekhten and the driving out of the evil spirit that was in\nher by Khensu-Nefer-hetep. The text of the Legend is cut in hieroglyphs\non a large sandstone tablet which was discovered by J.F. Champollion in\nthe temple of Khensu at Thebes, and was removed by Prisse d'Avennes in\n1846 to Paris, where it is now preserved in the Bibliothèque Nationale.\nThe form of the Legend which we have is probably the work of the priests\nof Khensu, about 1000 B.C., who wished to magnify their god, but the\nincidents recorded are supposed to have taken place at the end of the\nfourteenth century B.C., and there may indeed be historical facts\nunderlying the Legend. The text states that the king of Egypt,\nUsermaatra-setepenra Rameses-meri-Amen, _i.e._ Rameses II, a king of the\nnineteenth dynasty about 1300 B.C., was in the country of Nehern, or\nMesopotamia, according to his yearly custom, and that the chiefs of the\ncountry, even those of the remotest districts from Egypt, came to do\nhomage to him, and to bring him gifts, _i.e._ to pay tribute. Their\ngifts consisted of gold, lapis-lazuli, turquoise, and costly woods from\nthe land of the god,[1] and each chief tried to outdo his neighbour in\nthe magnificence of his gifts. Among these tributary chiefs was the\nPrince of Bekhten, who, in addition to his usual gift, presented to the\nking his eldest daughter, and he spake words of praise to the king, and\nprayed for his life. His daughter was beautiful, and the king thought\nher the most beautiful maiden in the world, and he gave her the name of\nNeferu-Ra and the rank of \"chief royal wife,\" _i.e._ the chief wife of\nPharaoh. When His Majesty brought her to Egypt she was treated as the\nQueen of Egypt.\n\n[Footnote: 1: _i.e._ Southern Arabia and a portion of the east coast of\nAfrica near Somaliland.]\n\nOne day in the late summer, in the fifteenth year of his reign, his\nMajesty was in Thebes celebrating a festival in honour of Father Amen,\nthe King of the gods, in the temple now known as the Temple of Luxor,\nwhen an official came and informed the king that \"an ambassador of the\nPrince of Bekhten had arrived bearing many gifts for the Royal Wife.\"\nThe ambassador was brought into the presence with his gifts, and having\naddressed the king in suitable words of honour, and smelt the ground\nbefore His Majesty, he told him that he had come to present a petition\nto him on behalf of the Queen's sister, who was called Bentresht (_i.e._\ndaughter of joy). The princess had been attacked by a disease, and the\nPrince of Bekhten asked His Majesty to send a skilled physician to see\nher. Straightway the king ordered his magicians (or medicine men) to\nappear before him, and also his nobles, and when they came he told them\nthat he had sent for them to come and hear the ambassador's request.\nAnd, he added, choose one of your number who is both wise and skilful;\ntheir choice fell upon the royal scribe Tehuti-em-heb, and the king\nordered him to depart to Bekhten to heal the princess. When the magician\narrived in Bekhten he found that Princess Bentresht was under the\ninfluence of a malignant spirit, and that this spirit refused to be\ninfluenced in any way by him; in fact all his wisdom and skill availed\nnothing, for the spirit was hostile to him."
}

  "passage_text": "Then the Prince of Bekhten sent a second messenger to His Majesty,\nbeseeching him to send a god to Bekhten to overcome the evil spirit, and\nhe arrived in Egypt nine years after the arrival of the first\nambassador. Again the king was celebrating a festival of Amen, and when\nhe heard of the request of the Prince of Bekhten he went and stood\nbefore the statue of Khensu, called \"Nefer-hetep,\" and he said, \"O my\nfair lord, I present myself a second time before thee on behalf of the\ndaughter of the Prince of Bekhten.\" He then went on to ask the god to\ntransmit his power to Khensu, \"Pa-ari-sekher-em-Uast,\" the god who\ndrives out the evil spirits which attack men, and to permit him to go to\nBekhten and release the Princess from the power of the evil spirit. And\nthe statue of Khensu Nefer-hetep bowed its head twice at each part of\nthe petition, and this god bestowed a fourfold portion of his spirit and\npower on Khensu Pa-ari-sekher-em-Uast. Then the king ordered that the\ngod should set out on his journey to Bekhten carried in a boat, which\nwas accompanied by five smaller boats and by chariots and horses. The\njourney occupied seventeen months, and the god was welcomed on his\narrival by the Prince of Bekhten and his nobles with suitable homage and\nmany cries of joy. The god was taken to the place where Princess\nBentresht was, and he used his magical power upon her with such good\neffect that she was made whole at once. The evil spirit who had\npossessed her came out of her and said to Khensu: \"Welcome, welcome, O\ngreat god, who dost drive away the spirits who attack men. Bekhten is\nthine; its people, both men and women, are thy servants, and I myself am\nthy servant. I am going to depart to the place whence I came, so that\nthy heart may be content concerning the matter about which thou hast\ncome. I beseech Thy Majesty to give the order that thou and I and the\nPrince of Bekhten may celebrate a festival together.\" The god Khensu\nbowed his head as a sign that he approved of the proposal, and told his\npriest to make arrangements with the Prince of Bekhten for offering up\na great offering. Whilst this conversation was passing between the evil\nspirit and the god the soldiers stood by in a state of great fear. The\nPrince of Bekhten made the great offering before Khensu and the evil\nspirit, and the Prince and the god and the spirit rejoiced greatly. When\nthe festival was ended the evil spirit, by the command of Khensu,\n\"departed to the place which he loved.\" The Prince and all his people\nwere immeasurably glad at the happy result, and he decided that he would\nconsider the god to be a gift to him, and that he would not let him\nreturn to Egypt. So the god Khensu stayed for three years and nine\nmonths in Bekhten, but one day, whilst the Prince was sleeping on his\nbed, he had a vision in which he saw Khensu in the form of a hawk leave\nhis shrine and mount up into the air, and then depart to Egypt. When he\nawoke he said to the priest of Khensu, \"The god who was staying with us\nhath departed to Egypt; let his chariot also depart.\" And the Prince\nsent off the statue of the god to Egypt, with rich gifts of all kinds\nand a large escort of soldiers and horses. In due course the party\narrived in Egypt, and ascended to Thebes, and the god Khensu\nPa-ari-sekher-em-Uast went into the temple of Khensu Nefer-hetep, and\nlaid all the gifts which he had received from the Prince of Bekhten\nbefore him, and kept nothing for his own temple. This he did as a proper\nact of gratitude to Khensu Nefer-hetep, whose gift of a fourfold portion\nof his spirit had enabled him to overcome the power of the evil spirit\nthat possessed the Princess of Bekhten. Thus Khensu returned from\nBekhten in safety, and he re-entered his temple in the winter, in the\nthirty-third year of the reign of Rameses II. The situation of Bekhten\nis unknown, but the name is probably not imaginary, and the country was\nperhaps a part of Western Asia. The time occupied by the god Khensu in\ngetting there does not necessarily indicate that Bekhten was a very long\nway off, for a mission of the kind moved slowly in those leisurely days,\nand the priest of the god would probably be much delayed by the people\nin the towns and villages on the way, who would entreat him to ask the\ngod to work cures on the diseased and afflicted that were brought to\nhim. We must remember that when the Nubians made a treaty with\nDiocletian they stipulated that the goddess Isis should be allowed to\nleave her temple once a year, and to make a progress through the country\nso that men and women might ask her for boons, and receive them."

  "passage_text": "CHAPTER VIII

                         HISTORICAL LITERATURE

The historical period of Egyptian history, that is to say, the period
during which Egypt was ruled by kings, each one calling himself
NESU-BATI, or "King of the South, King of the North," covers about 4400
years according to some Egyptologists, and 3300 years according to
others. Of the kings of All Egypt who reigned during the period we know
the names of about two hundred, but only about one hundred and fifty
have left behind them monuments that enable us to judge of their power
and greatness. There is no evidence to show that the Egyptians ever
wrote history in our sense of the word, and there is not in existence
any native work that can be regarded as a history of Egypt. The only
known attempt in ancient times to write a history of Egypt was that made
by Manetho, a skilled scribe and learned man, who, in the reign of
Ptolemy II Philadelphus (289-246 B.C.), undertook to write a history of
the country, which was to be placed in the Great Library at Alexandria.
The only portion of this History that has come down to us is the List of
Kings, which formed a section of it; this List, in a form more or less
accurate, is extant in the works of Africanus and Eusebius. According to
the former 553 or 554 kings ruled over Egypt in 5380 years, and
according to the latter 421 or 423 kings ruled over Egypt in 4547 or
4939 years. It is quite certain that the principal acts and wars of each
king were recorded by the court scribes, or official "remembrancer" or
"recorder" of the day, and there is no doubt that such records were
preserved in the "House of Books," or Library, of the local temple for
reference if necessary. If this were not so it would have been
impossible for the scribes of the eighteenth and nineteenth dynasties to
compile the lists of kings found on the Palermo Stone, and in the Turin
Papyrus, and on the Tablets set up by Seti I and Rameses II at Abydos,
and on the Tablet of Ancestors at Karnak. These Lists, however, seem to
show that the learned scribes of the later period were not always sure
of the true sequence of the names, and that when they were dealing with
the names of the kings of the first two dynasties they were not always
certain even about the correct spelling and reading of their names. The
reason why the Egyptians did not write the history of their country from
a general point of view is easily explained. Each king wished to be
thought as great as possible, and each king's courtiers lost no
opportunity of showing that they believed him to be the greatest king
who had sat on the throne of Egypt. To magnify the deeds of his
ancestors was neither politic nor safe, nor did it lead to favours or
promotion. In no inscription of their descendants do we find the mighty
deeds and great conquests of Amenemhat III, or of Usertsen III, or of
Thothmes III, praised or described, and no court scribe ever dared to
draft a text stating that these were truly three of the greatest kings
of Egypt. When a local chief succeeded in making himself king of All
Egypt he did not concern himself with preserving records of the great
deeds of the king whose throne he had seized. When foreign foes invaded
Egypt and conquered it their followers raided the towns, burnt and
destroyed all that could be got rid of, and smashed the monuments
recording the prowess of the king they had overthrown. The net result of
all this is that the history of Egypt can only be partially constructed,
and that the sources of our information are a series of texts that were
written to glorify individual kings, and not to describe the history of
a dynasty, or the general development of the country, or the working out
of a policy. In attempting to draw up a connected account of a reign or
period the funerary inscriptions of high officials are often more useful
than the royal inscriptions. In the following pages are given extracts
from annals, building inscriptions, narratives of conquests, and
"triumph inscriptions" of an official character; specimens of the
funerary inscriptions that describe military expeditions, and supply
valuable information about the general history of events, will be given
in the chapter on Biographical Inscriptions.

The earliest known annals are found on a stone which is preserved in the
Museum at Palermo, and which for this reason is called "The Palermo
Stone"; the Egyptian text was first published by Signor A. Pellegrini in
1896. How the principal events of certain years of the reigns of kings
from the Predynastic Period to the middle of the fifth dynasty are noted
is shown by the following:

    [Reign of] SENEFERU. Year ...

    The building of Tuataua ships of _mer_ wood of a hundred capacity,
    and 60 royal boats of sixteen capacity.

    Raid in the Land of the Blacks (_i.e._ the Sudan), and the bringing
    in of seven thousand prisoners, men and women, and twenty thousand
    cattle, sheep, and goats.

    Building of the Wall of the South and North [called] House of
    Seneferu.

    The bringing of forty ships of cedar wood (or perhaps "laden with
    cedar wood").

    [Height of the Nile.] Two cubits, two fingers.

    [Reign of Seneferu.] Year ...

    The making of thirty-five ... 122 cattle

    The construction of one Tuataua ship of cedar wood of a hundred
    capacity, and two ships of _mer_ wood of a hundred capacity.

    The numbering for the seventh time.

    [Height of the Nile.] Five cubits, one hand, one finger.

The royal historical inscriptions of the first eleven dynasties are very
few, and their contents are meagre and unimportant. As specimens of
historical documents of the twelfth dynasty the following may be quoted:"

  "passage_text": "EDICT AGAINST THE BLACKS\n\nThis short inscription is dated in the eighth year of the reign of\nUsertsen III. \"The southern frontier in the eighth year under the\nMajesty of the King of the South and North, Khakaura (Usertsen III),\nendowed with life for ever. No Black whatsoever shall be permitted to\npass [this stone] going down stream, whether travelling by land or\nsailing in a boat, with cattle, asses, goats, &c., belonging to the\nBlacks, with the exception of such as cometh to do business in the\ncountry of Aqen[1] or on an embassy. Such, however, shall be well\nentreated in every way. No boats belonging to the Blacks shall in future\nbe permitted to pass down the river by the region of Heh.\"[2]\n\n[Footnote 1: This district has not been identified.]\n\n[Footnote 2: The district of Semnah and Kummah, about 40 miles south of\nWadi Halfah.]\n\nThe methods of Usertsen III and his opinions of the Sudani folk are\nillustrated by the following inscription which he set up at Semnah, a\nfort built by him at the foot of the Second Cataract.\n\n\"In the third month[1] of the season Pert His Majesty fixed the boundary\nof Egypt on the south at Heh (Semnah). I made my boundary and went\nfurther up the river than my fathers. I added greatly to it. I give\ncommands [therein]. I am the king, and what is said by me is done. What\nmy heart conceiveth my hand bringeth to pass. I am [like] the crocodile\nwhich seizeth, carrieth off, and destroyeth without mercy. Words (or\nmatters) do not remain dormant in my heart. To the coward soft talk\nsuggesteth longsuffering; this I give not to my enemies. Him who\nattacketh me I attack. I am silent in the matter that is for silence; I\nanswer as the matter demandeth. Silence after an attack maketh the heart\nof the enemy bold. The attack must be sudden like that of a crocodile.\nThe man who hesitateth is a coward, and a wretched creature is he who is\ndefeated on his own territory and turned into a slave. The Black\nunderstandeth talk only. Speak to him and he falleth prostrate. He\nfleeth before a pursuer, and he pursueth only him that fleeth. The\nBlacks are not bold men; on the contrary, they are timid and weak, and\ntheir hearts are cowed. My Majesty hath seen them, and [what I say] is\nno lie.\n\n[Footnote 1: = January-February.]\n\n\"I seized their women, I carried off their workers in the fields, I came\nto their wells, I slew their bulls, I cut their corn and I burnt it.\nThis I swear by the life of my father. I speak the truth; there is no\ndoubt about the matter, and that which cometh forth from my mouth cannot\nbe gainsaid. Furthermore, every son of mine who shall keep intact this\nboundary which My Majesty hath made, is indeed my son; he is the son who\nprotecteth his father, if he keep intact the boundary of him that begot\nhim. He who shall allow this boundary to be removed, and shall not fight\nfor it, is not my son, and he hath not been begotten by me. Moreover, My\nMajesty hath caused to be made a statue of My Majesty on this my\nboundary, not only with the desire that ye should prosper thereby, but\nthat ye should do battle for it.\""
}

The opening lines enumerate the names and titles of the king, and\nproclaim his sovereignty over the Haunebu, or the dwellers in the\nnorthern Delta and on the sea coast, Upper and Lower Egypt, Nubia and\nthe Eastern Desert, including Sinai, Syria, the lands of the Fenkhu, and\nthe countries that lie to the south of the modern town of Khartum.   "passage_text": "CAPTURE OF MEGIDDO BY THOTHMES III

The following is the official account of the Battle of Megiddo in Syria,
which was won by Thothmes III in the twenty-third year of his reign. The
narrative is taken from the Annals of Thothmes III. The king set out
from Thebes and marched into Syria, and received the submission of
several small towns, and having made his way with difficulty through the
hilly region to the south of the city of Megiddo, he camped there to
prepare for the battle. "Then the tents of His Majesty were pitched, and
orders were sent out to the whole army, saying, Arm yourselves, get your
weapons ready, for we shall set out to do battle with the miserable
enemy at daybreak. The king sat in his tent, the officers made their
preparations, and the rations of the servants were provided. The
military sentries went about crying, Be firm of heart. Be firm of heart.
Keep watch, keep watch. Keep watch over the life of the king in his
tent. And a report was brought to His Majesty that the country was
quiet, and that the foot soldiers of the south and north were ready. On
the twenty-first day of the first month of the season Shemu
(March-April) of the twenty-third year of the reign of His Majesty, and
the day of the festival of the new moon, which was also the anniversary
of the king's coronation, at dawn, behold, the order was given to set
the whole army in motion. His Majesty set out in his chariot of
silver-gold, and he had girded on himself the weapons of battle, like
Horus the Slayer, the lord of might, and he was like unto Menthu [the
War-god] of Thebes, and Amen his father gave strength to his arms. The
southern half of the army was stationed on a hill to the south of the
stream Kina, and the northern half lay to the south-west of Megiddo; His
Majesty was between them, and Amen was protecting him and giving
strength to his body. His Majesty at the head of his army attacked his
enemies, and broke their line, and when they saw that he was
overwhelming them they broke and fled to Megiddo in a panic, leaving
their horses and their gold and silver chariots on the field. [The
fugitives] were pulled up by the people over the walls into the city;
now they let down their clothes by which to pull them up. If the
soldiers of His Majesty had not devoted themselves to securing loot of
the enemy, they would have been able to capture the city of Megiddo at
the moment when the vile foes from Kadesh and the vile foes from this
city were being dragged up hurriedly over the walls into this city; for
the terror of His Majesty had entered into them, and their arms dropped
helplessly, and the serpent on his crown overthrew them. Their horses
and their chariots [which were decorated] with gold and silver were
seized as spoil, and their mighty men of war lay stretched out dead upon
the ground like fishes, and the conquering soldiers of His Majesty went
about counting their shares. And behold, the tent of the vile chief of
the enemy, wherein was his son, was also captured. Then all the soldiers
rejoiced greatly, and they glorified Amen, because he had made his son
(_i.e._ the king) victorious on that day, and they praised His Majesty
greatly, and acclaimed his triumph. And they collected the loot which
they had taken, viz. hands [cut off the dead], prisoners, horses,
chariots [decorated with] gold and silver," etc.

In spite of the joy of the army Thothmes was angry with his troops for
having failed to capture the city. Every rebel chief was in Megiddo, and
its capture would have been worth more than the capture of a thousand
other cities, for he could have slain all the rebel chiefs, and the
revolt would have collapsed completely. Thothmes then laid siege to the
city, and he threw up a strong wall round about it, through which none
might pass, and the daily progress of the siege was recorded on a
leather roll, which was subsequently preserved in the temple of Amen at
Thebes. After a time the chiefs in Megiddo left their city and advanced
to the gate in the siege-wall and reported that they had come to tender
their submission to His Majesty, and it was accepted. They brought to
him rich gifts of gold, silver, lapis-lazuli, turquoise, wheat, wine,
cattle, sheep, goats, &c., and he reappointed many of the penitent
chiefs to their former towns as vassals of Egypt. Among the gifts were
340 prisoners, 83 hands, 2041 mares, 191 foals, 6 stallions, a royal
chariot with a golden pole, a second royal chariot, 892 chariots, total
924 chariots; 2 royal coats of mail, 200 ordinary coats of mail, 502
bows, 7 tent poles inlaid with gold, 1929 cattle, 2000 goats, and 20,500
sheep.

              THE CONQUESTS OF THOTHMES III SUMMARISED BY
                        AMEN-RA, KING OF THE GODS

The conquests of Thothmes III were indeed splendid achievements, and the
scribes of his time summarised them very skilfully in a fine text which
they had cut in hieroglyphs on a large stele at Karnak. The treatment
is, of course, somewhat poetical, but there are enough historical facts
underlying the statements to justify a rendering of it being given in
this chapter. The text is supposed to be a speech of Amen-Ra, the lord
of the thrones of the Two Lands, to the king. He says:"
}

  "passage_text": ""Thou hast come to me, thou hast rejoiced in beholding my beneficence, O
my son, my advocate, Menkheperra, living for ever! I rise upon thee
through my love for thee. My heart rejoiceth at thy auspicious comings
to my temple. My hands knit together thy limbs with the fluid of life;
sweet unto me are thy gracious acts towards my person. I have stablished
thee in my sanctuary. I have made thee to be a source of wonder [to
men]. I have given unto thee strength and conquests over all lands. I
have set thy Souls and the fear of thee in all lands. The terror of thee
hath penetrated to the four pillars of the sky. I have made great the
awe of thee in all bodies. I have set the roar of Thy Majesty everywhere
[in the lands of] the Nine Bows (_i.e._ Nubia). The Chiefs of all lands
are grouped in a bunch within thy fist. I put out my two hands; I tied
them in a bundle for thee. I collected the Antiu of Ta-sti[1] in tens of
thousands and thousands, and I made captives by the hundred thousand of
the Northern Nations. I have cast down thy foes under thy sandals, thou
hast trampled upon the hateful and vile-hearted foes even as I commanded
thee. The length and breadth of the earth are thine, and those who dwell
in the East and the West are vassals unto thee. Thou hast trodden upon
all countries, thy heart is expanded (_i.e._ glad). No one dareth to
approach Thy Majesty with hostility, because I am thy guide to conduct
thee to them. Thou didst sail over the Great Circuit of water (the
Euphrates) of Nehren (Aram Naharayim, or Mesopotamia) with strength and
power. I have commanded for thee that they should hear thy roarings, and
run away into holes in the ground. I stopped up their nostrils [shutting
out] the breath of life. I have set the victories of Thy Majesty in
their minds. The fiery serpent Khut which is on thy forehead burnt them
up. It made thee to grasp as an easy prey the Ketu peoples, it burnt up
the dwellers in their marshes with its fire. The Princes of the Aamu
(Asiatics) have been slaughtered, not one of them remains, and the sons
of the mighty men have fallen. I have made thy mighty deeds to go
throughout all lands, the serpent on my crown hath illumined thy
territory, nothing that is an abomination unto thee existeth in all the
wide heaven, and the people come bearing offerings upon their backs,
bowing to the ground before Thy Majesty, in accordance with my decree. I
made impotent those who dared to attack thee, their hearts melted and
their limbs quaked.

[Footnote 1: The natives of the Eastern Desert of Nubia.]

"I have come, making thee to trample under foot the Chief of Tchah
(Syria), I have cast them down under thy feet in all the lands, I have
made them to behold Thy Majesty as the 'lord of beams' (_i.e._ the
Sun-god), thou hast shone on their faces as the image of me.

"I have come, making thee to trample under foot the people of Asia, thou
hast led away captive the Chiefs of the Aamu of Retenu, I have made them
to behold Thy Majesty arrayed in thy decorations, grasping the weapons
for battle, [mounted] on thy chariot.

"I have come, making thee to trample under foot the land of the East,
thou hast trodden upon those who dwell in the districts of the Land of
the God, I have made them to see thee as the brilliant star that
shooteth out light and fire and scattereth its dew.

"I have come, making thee to trample under foot the land of the West,
Kefti (Phoenicia) and Asi (Cyprus) are in awe of thee. I have made them
to see Thy Majesty as a young bull, steady-hearted, with horns ready to
strike, invincible.

"I have come, making thee to trample under foot those who are in their
marshes, the Lands of Methen (Mitani) quake through their fear of thee.
I have made them to see Thy Majesty as the crocodile, the lord of terror
in the water, unassailable.

"I have come, making thee to trample under foot those who dwell in the
Islands, those who live in the Great Green (Mediterranean) hear thy
roarings, I have made them to see Thy Majesty as the slayer when he
mounteth on the back of his sacrificial animal.

"I have come, making thee to trample under foot the Thehenu (Libyans),
the Islands of the Uthentiu [have submitted to] the power of thy Souls.
I have made them to see Thy Majesty as a savage lion, which hath
scattered the dead bodies of the people throughout their valleys.

"I have come, making thee to trample under foot the uttermost ends of
the earth, the Circuit of the Great Circuit is in thy grasp, I have made
them to see Thy Majesty as the hawk, which seizeth what it seeth when it
pleaseth.

"I have come, making thee to trample upon those who are on their
frontiers(?), thou hast smitten 'those on their sand' (_i.e._ the desert
dwellers), making them living captives. I have made them to see Thy
Majesty as a jackal of the south, moving fleetly and stealthily, and
traversing the Two Lands.

"I have come, making thee to trample under foot the Antiu of Ta-sti, as
far as ... they are in thy grasp. I have made them to see Thy Majesty as
the Two Brothers (Set and Horus), I have gathered together their arms
about thee with [strength].

"I have placed thy Two Sisters (Isis and Nephthys) near thee as
protectresses for thee, the arms of Thy Majesty are [lifted] upwards to
drive away evil. I have made thee strong and glorious, O my beloved Son,
thou Mighty Bull, crowned in Thebes, begotten by me ..., Thothmes, the
everliving, who hast performed for me all that my Ka wished. Thou hast
set up my sanctuary with work that shall endure for ever, thou hast
lengthened it and broadened it more than ever was done before. The great
pylon ... Thou hast celebrated the festival of the beauties of Amen-Ra,
thy monuments are greater than those of any king who hath existed, I
commanded thee to do it. I am satisfied with it. I have stablished thee
upon the throne of Horus for hundreds of thousands of years. Thou shalt
guide life ...""
}

  "passage_text": "SUMMARY OF THE REIGN OF RAMESES III\n\nThe reign of Rameses III is remarkable in the annals of the New Empire,\nand the great works which this king carried out, and his princely\nbenefactions to the temples of Egypt, are described at great length in\nhis famous papyrus in the British Museum (Harris, No. 1, No. 9999). The\nlast section of the papyrus contains an excellent historical summary of\nthe reign of Rameses III, and as it is one of the finest examples of\nthis class of literature a translation of it is here given. The text is\nwritten in the hieratic character and reads:\n\nKing Usermaatra-meri-Amen (Rameses III), life, strength, health [be to\nhim!] the great god, said unto the princes, and the chiefs of the land,\nand the soldiers, and the charioteers, and the Shartanau soldiers, and\nthe multitudes of the bowmen, and all those who lived in the land of\nTa-mera (Egypt), Hearken ye, and I will cause you to know the splendid\ndeeds which I did when I was king of men. The land of Kamt was laid open\nto the foreigner, every man [was ejected] from his rightful holding,\nthere was no \"chief mouth\" (_i.e._ ruler) for many years in olden times\nuntil the new period [came]. The land of Egypt [was divided among]\nchiefs and governors of towns, each one slew his neighbour. ... Another\nperiod followed with years of nothingness (famine?). Arsu, a certain\nSyrian, was with them as governor, he made the whole land to be one\nholding before him. He collected his vassals, and mulcted them of their\npossessions heavily. They treated the gods as if they were men, and they\noffered up no propitiatory offerings in their temples. Now when the gods\nturned themselves back to peace, and to the restoration of what was\nright in the land, according to its accustomed and proper form, they\nestablished their son who proceeded from their body to be Governor,\nlife, strength, health [be to him!], of every land, upon their great\nthrone, namely, Userkhara-setep-en-Amen-meri-Amen, life strength, health\n[be to him!], the son of Ra, Set-nekht-merr-Ra-meri-Amen, life,\nstrength, health [be to him!]. He was like Khepra-Set when he is wroth.\nHe quieted the whole country which had been in rebellion. He slew the\nevil-hearted ones who were in Ta-mera (Egypt). He purified the great\nthrone of Egypt. He was the Governor, life, strength, health [be to\nhim!], of the Two Lands, on the throne of Amen. He made to appear the\nfaces that had withdrawn themselves. Of those who had been behind walls\nevery man recognised his fellow. He endowed the temples with offerings\nto offer as was right to the Nine Gods, according to use and wont. He\nmade me by a decree to be the Hereditary Chief in the seat of Keb. I\nbecame the \"Great High Mouth\" of the lands of Egypt, I directed the\naffairs of the whole land, which had been made one. He set on his double\nhorizon (_i.e._ he died) like the Nine Gods. There was performed for him\nwhat was performed for Osiris; sailing in his royal boat on the river,\nand resting [finally] in his house of eternity (_i.e._ the tomb) in\nWestern Thebes.\n\nMy father Amen, the lord of the gods, Ra, Tem, and Ptah of the Beautiful\nFace made me to be crowned lord of the Two Lands in the place of my\nbegetter. I received the rank of my father with cries of joy. The land\nhad peace, being fed with offerings, and men rejoiced in seeing me,\nGovernor, life, strength, health [be to him!], of the Two Lands, like\nHorus when he was made to be Governor of the Two Lands on the throne of\nOsiris. I was crowned with the Atef crown with the serpents, I bound on\nthe crown with plumes, like Tatenn. I sat on the throne of Heru-Khuti\n(Harmakhis). I was arrayed in the ornaments [of sovereignty] like Tem. I\nmade Ta-mera to possess many [different] kinds of men, the officers of\nthe palace, the great chiefs, large numbers of horse and chariot\nsoldiers, hundreds of thousands of them, the Shartanau and the Qehequ,\nwho were numberless, soldiers of the bodyguard in tens of thousands, and\nthe peasants belonging to Ta-mera.\n\nI enlarged all the frontiers of Egypt, I conquered those who crossed\nover them in their [own] lands. I slaughtered the Tanauna in their\nislands; the Thakra and the Purastau were made into a holocaust. The\nShartanau and the Uasheshu of the sea were made non-existent; they were\nseized [by me] at one time, and were brought as captives to Egypt, like\nthe sand in the furrows. I provided fortresses for them to dwell in, and\nthey were kept in check by my name. Their companies were very numerous,\nlike hundreds of thousands. I assessed every one of them for taxes\nyearly, in apparel and wheat from the stores and granaries. I crushed\nthe Saara and the tribes of the Shasu (nomad shepherds). I carried off\ntheir tents from their men, and the equipment thereof, and their flocks\nand herds likewise, which were without number. They were put in fetters\nand brought along as captives, as offerings to Egypt, and I gave them to\nthe Nine Gods as slaves for their temples."

  "passage_text": "Behold, I will also make you to know concerning the other schemes that\nhave been carried out in Ta-mera during my reign. The Labu (Libyans) and\nthe Mashuashau had made their dwelling in Egypt, for they had captured\nthe towns on the west bank of the Nile from Hetkaptah (Memphis) to\nQarabana. They had occupied also both banks of the \"Great River,\" and\nthey had been in possession of the towns (or villages) of Kutut[1] for\nvery, very many years whilst they were [lords] over Egypt. Behold, I\ncrushed them and slaughtered them at one time (_i.e._ in one\nengagement). I overthrew the Mashuashau, the Libyans, the Asbatau, the\nQaiqashau, the Shaiu, the Hasau, and the Baqanau. [I] slaughtered them\nin their blood, and they became piles of dead bodies. [Thus] I drove\nthem away from marching over the border of Egypt. The rest of them I\ncarried away, a vast multitude of prisoners, trussed like geese in front\nof my horses, their women and their children in tens of thousands, and\ntheir flocks and herds in hundreds of thousands. I allotted to their\nchiefs fortresses, and they lived there under my name. I made them\nofficers of the bowmen, and captains of the tribes; they were branded\nwith my name and became my slaves; their wives and their children were\nlikewise turned into slaves. Their flocks and herds I brought into the\nHouse of Amen, and they became his live-stock for ever.\n\n[Footnote 1: Perhaps the district of Canopus.]\n\nI made a very large well in the desert of Aina. It had a girdle wall\nlike a mountain of basalt(?), with twenty buttresses(?) in the\nfoundation [on] the ground, and its height was thirty cubits, and it had\nbastions. The frame-work and the doors were cut out of cedar, and the\nbolts thereof and their sockets were of copper. I cut out large\nsea-going boats, with smaller boats before them, and they were manned\nwith large crews, and large numbers of serving-men. With them were the\nofficers of the bowmen of the boats, and there were trained captains and\nmates to inspect them. They were loaded with the products of Egypt which\nwere without number, and they were in very large numbers, like tens of\nthousands. These were despatched to the Great Sea of the water of Qett\n(_i.e._ the Red Sea), they arrived at the lands of Punt, no disaster\nfollowed them, and they were in an effective state and were\nawe-inspiring. Both the large boats and the little boats were laden with\nthe products of the Land of the God, and with all kinds of wonderful and\nmysterious things which are produced in those lands, and with vast\nquantities of the _anti_ (myrrh) of Punt, which was loaded on to them by\ntens of thousands [of measures] that were without number. The sons of\nthe chief of the Land of the God went in front of their offerings, their\nfaces towards Egypt. They arrived and were sound and well at the\nmountain of Qebtit (Coptos),[1] they moored their boats in peace, with\nthe things which they had brought as offerings. To cross the desert they\nwere loaded upon asses and on [the backs of] men, and they were\n[re]loaded into river-barges at the quay of Coptos. They were despatched\ndown the river, they arrived during a festival, and some of the most\nwonderful of the offerings were carried into the presence of [My\nMajesty]. The children of their chiefs adored my face, they smelt the\nearth before my face, and rolled on the ground. I gave them to all the\ngods of this land to propitiate the two gods in front of me every\nmorning.\n\n[Footnote 1: _i.e._ the part at the Red Sea end of the Valley of\nHammamat.]\n\nI despatched my envoys to the desert of Aataka to the great copper\nworkings that are in this place. Their sea-going boats were laden with\n[some of] them, whilst those who went through the desert rode on asses.\nSuch a thing as this was never heard of before, from the time when kings\nbegan to reign. Their copper workings were found, and they were full of\ncopper, and the metal was loaded by ten thousands [of measures] into\ntheir sea-going boats. They were despatched with their faces towards\nEgypt, and they arrived safely. The metal was lifted out and piled up\nunder the veranda in the form of blocks (or ingots) of copper, vast\nnumbers of them, as it were tens of thousands. They were in colour like\ngold of three refinings. I allowed everybody to see them, as they were\nwonderful things.\n\nI despatched inspectors and overseers to the turquoise desert (_i.e._\nSinai) of my mother, the goddess Hathor, the lady of the turquoise.\n[They] carried to her silver, gold, byssus, fine (?) linen, and many\nthings as numerous as the sand-grains, and laid them before her. And\nthere were brought unto me most wonderfully fine turquoises, real\nstones, in large numbers of bags, and laid out before me. The like had\nnever been seen before--since kings began to reign."
}

  "passage_text": "I caused the whole country to be planted with groves of trees and with\nflowering shrubs, and I made the people to sit under the shade thereof.\nI made it possible for an Egyptian woman to walk with a bold step to the\nplace whither she wished to go; no strange man attacked her, and no one\non the road. I made the foot-soldiers and the charioteers sit down in my\ntime, and the Shartanau and the Qehequ were in their towns lying at full\nlength on their backs; they were unafraid, for there was no fighting man\n[to come] from Kash (Nubia), [and no] enemy from Syria. Their bows and\ntheir weapons of war lay idle in their barracks, and they ate their\nfill and drank their fill with shouts of joy. Their wives were with\nthem, [their] children were by their side; there was no need to keep\ntheir eyes looking about them, their hearts were bold, for I was with\nthem as strength and protection for their bodies. I kept alive (_i.e._\nfed) the whole country, aliens, artisans, gentle and simple, men and\nwomen. I delivered a man from his foe and I gave him air. I rescued him\nfrom the strong man, him who was more honourable than the strong man. I\nmade all men to have their rightful positions in their towns. Some I\nmade to live [taking them] in the very chamber of the Tuat.[1] Where the\nland was bare I covered it over again; the land was well filled during\nmy reign. I performed deeds of beneficence towards the gods as well as\ntowards men; I had no property that belonged to the people. I served my\noffice of king upon earth, as Governor of the Two Lands, and ye were\nslaves under my feet without [complaint ?]. Ye were satisfactory to my\nheart, as were your good actions, and ye performed my decrees and my\nwords.\n\n[Footnote 1: The sick and needy who were at death's door.]\n\nBehold, I have set in Akert (the Other World) like my father Ra. I am\namong the Great Companies of the gods of heaven, earth, and the Tuat.\nAmen-Ra hath stablished my son upon my throne, he hath received my rank\nin peace, as Governor of the Two Lands, and he is sitting upon the\nthrone of Horus as Lord of the Two Nile-banks. He hath put on himself\nthe Atef crown like Ta-Tenn, Usermaatra-setep-en-Amen, life, strength,\nhealth [be to him!], the eldest-born son of Ra, the self-begotten,\nRameses (IV)-heqmaat-meri-Amen, life, strength, health [be to him!], the\ndivine child, the son of Amen, who came forth from his body, rising as\nthe Lord of the Two Lands, like Ta-Tenn. He is like a real son, favoured\nfor his father's sake. Tie ye yourselves to his sandals. Smell the earth\nbefore him. Do homage to him. Follow him at every moment. Praise him.\nWorship him. Magnify his beneficent actions as ye do those of Ra every\nmorning. Present ye before him your offerings [in] his Great House\n(_i.e._ palace), which is holy. Carry ye to him the \"blessings\" (?) of\nthe [tilled] lands and the deserts. Be strong to fulfil his words and\nthe decrees that are uttered among you. Follow (?) his utterances, and\nye shall be safe under his Souls. Work all together for him in every\nwork. Haul monuments for him, excavate canals for him, work for him in\nthe work of your hands, and there will accrue unto you his favour as\nwell as his food daily. Amen hath decreed for him his sovereignty upon\nearth, he hath made this period of his life twice as long as that of any\nother king, the King of the South and North, the Lord of the Two Lands,\nUsermaatra-setep-en-Amen, life, strength, health [be to him!], the son\nof Ra, the lord of crowns, Rameses (IV)-heqmaat-meri-Amen, life,\nstrength, health [be to him!], who is endowed with life for ever.\n\n                   THE INVASION AND CONQUEST OF EGYPT\n                        BY PIANKHI, KING OF NUBIA\n\nThe text describing the invasion and conquest of Egypt by Piankhi, King\nof Nubia, is cut in hieroglyphs upon a massive stone stele which was\nfound among the ruins of Piankhi's temple at Gebel Barkal, near the foot\nof the Fourth Cataract, and which is now preserved in the Egyptian\nMuseum, Cairo. Although this composition does not belong to the best\nperiod of Egyptian Literature, it is a very fine work. The narrative is\nvivid, and the aim of the writer was rather to state the facts of this\nsplendid expedition than to heap up empty compliments on the king; both\nthe subject-matter and the dress in which it appears are well worthy of\nreproduction in an English form. The inscription is dated in the\ntwenty-first year of Piankhi's reign, and the king says:"

  "passage_text": "\"Hearken ye to [the account of] what I have done more than my ancestors.\nI am a king, the emanation of the god, the living offspring of the god\nTem, who at birth was ordained the Governor whom princes were to fear.\"\nHis mother knew before his birth that he was to be the Governor, he the\nbeneficent god, the beloved of the gods, the son of Ra who was made by\nhis (the god's) hands, Piankhi-meri-Amen. One came and reported to His\nMajesty that the great prince Tafnekht had taken possession of all the\ncountry on the west bank of the Nile in the Delta, from the swamps even\nto Athi-taui[1], that he had sailed up the river with a large force,\nthat all the people on both sides of the river had attached themselves\nto him, and that all the princes and governors and heads of temple-towns\nhad flocked to him, and that they were \"about his feet like dogs.\" No\ncity had shut its gates before him, on the contrary, Mer-Tem,\nPer-sekhem-kheper-Ra, Het-neter-Sebek, Per-Metchet, Thekansh, and all\nthe towns in the west had opened their gates to him. In the east\nHet-benu, Taiutchait, Het-suten, and Pernebtepahet had opened to him,\nand he had besieged Hensu (Herakleopolis) and closely invested it. He\nhad enclosed it like a serpent with its tail in its mouth. \"Those who\nwould come out he will not allow to come out, and those who would go in\nhe will not allow to go in, by reason of the fighting that taketh place\nevery day. He hath thrown soldiers round about it everywhere.\" Piankhi\nlistened to the report undismayed, and he smiled, for his heart was\nglad. Presently further reports of the uprising came, and the king\nlearned that Nemart, another great prince, had joined his forces to\nthose of Tafnekht. Nemart had thrown down the fortifications of Nefrus,\nhe had laid waste his own town, and had thrown off his allegiance to\nPiankhi completely.\n\n[Footnote 1: A fortress a few miles south of Memphis.]\n\nThen Piankhi sent orders to Puarma and Las(?)-mer-sekni, the Nubian\ngenerals stationed in Egypt, and told them to assemble the troops, to\nseize the territory of Hermopolis, to besiege the city itself, to seize\nall the people, and cattle, and the boats on the river, and to stop all\nthe agricultural operations that were going on; these orders were\nobeyed. At the same time he despatched a body of troops to Egypt, with\ncareful instructions as to the way in which they were to fight, and he\nbade them remember that they were fighting under the protection of Amen.\nHe added, \"When ye arrive at Thebes, opposite the Apts,[1] go into the\nwaters of the river and wash yourselves, then array yourselves in your\nfinest apparel, unstring your bows, and lay down your spears. Let no\nchief imagine that he is as strong as the Lord of strength (_i.e._\nAmen), for without him there is no strength. The weak of arm he maketh\nstrong of arm. Though the enemy be many they shall turn their backs in\nflight before the weak man, and one shall take captive a thousand. Wet\nyourselves with the water of his altars, smell the earth before him, and\nsay: O make a way for us! Let us fight under the shadow of thy sword,\nfor a child, if he be but sent forth by thee, shall vanquish multitudes\nwhen he attacketh.\" Then the soldiers threw themselves flat on their\nfaces before His Majesty, saying, \"Behold, thy name breedeth strength in\nus. Thy counsel guideth thy soldiers into port (_i.e._ to success). Thy\nbread is in our bodies on every road, thy beer quencheth our thirst.\nBehold, thy bravery hath given us strength, and at the mere mention of\nthy name there shall be victory. The soldiers who are led by a coward\ncannot stand firm. Who is like unto thee? Thou art the mighty king who\nworkest with thy hands, thou art a master of the operations of war.\"\n\n[Footnote 1: _i.e._ the temples of Karnak and Luxor.]\n\n\"Then the soldiers set out on their journey, and they sailed down the\nriver and arrived at Thebes, and they did everything according to His\nMajesty's commands. And again they set out, and they sailed down the\nriver, and they met many large boats sailing up the river, and they were\nfull of soldiers and sailors, and mighty captains from the North land,\nevery one fully armed to fight, and the soldiers of His Majesty\ninflicted a great defeat on them; they killed a very large but unknown\nnumber, they captured the boats, made the soldiers prisoners, whom they\nbrought alive to the place where His Majesty was.\" This done they\nproceeded on their way to the region opposite Herakleopolis, to continue\nthe battle. Again the soldiers of Piankhi attacked the troops of the\nallies, and defeated and routed them utterly, and captured their boats\non the river. A large number of the enemy succeeded in escaping, and\nlanded on the west bank of the river at Per-pek. At dawn these were\nattacked by Piankhi's troops, who slew large numbers of them, and\n[captured] many horses; the remainder, utterly terror-stricken, fled\nnorthwards, carrying with them the news of the worst defeat which they\nhad ever experienced."
}
