  "passage_text": "III. The BOOK OF GATES.--This book was also written to be a Guide to the\nTuat, and has much in common with the Book of the Two Ways and with the\nBook Am Tuat. In it also the Tuat is divided into ten sections and has\ntwo vestibules, the Eastern and the Western, but at the entrance to each\nsection is a strongly fortified Gate, guarded by a monster serpent-god\nand by the gods of the section. The Sun-god of night, as in the Book Am\nTuat, makes his journey in a boat, and is attended by a number of gods,\nwho remove all opposition from his path by the use of words of power. As\nhe approaches each Gate, its doors are thrown open by the gods who guard\nthem, and he passes into the section of the Tuat behind it, carrying\nwith him light, air, and food for its inhabitants. The Book of Gates\nembodies the teaching of the priests of the cult of Osiris, and the Book\nAm Tuat represents the modified form of it that was promulgated by the\npriests of Amen. From the Book of Gates we derive much information about\nthe realm of Osiris, and the Great Judgment of souls, which took place\nin his Hall of Judgment once a day at midnight. Then all the souls that\nhad collected during the past twenty-four hours from all parts of Egypt\nwere weighed in the Balance; the righteous were allotted estates in\nperpetuity in the \"land of souls,\" and the wicked were destroyed by\nShesmu, the executioner of the god, and by his assistants. The texts\nthat describe the various \"Gates\" of the Book of Gates, explain who are\nthe beings represented in the pictures, and state why they were there.\nAnd the Book proves conclusively that the Egyptians believed in the\nefficacy of sacrifices and offerings, and in the doctrine of righteous\nretribution; liars and deceivers were condemned, and their bodies,\nsouls, spirits, doubles, and names destroyed, and the righteous were\nrewarded for their upright lives and integrity upon earth by the gift of\neverlasting life and happiness. The most complete copy of this\ninteresting work in England is cut on the alabaster sarcophagus of Seti\nI, about 1350 B.C. This unique sepulchral monument is exhibited gratis\nin Sir John Soane's Museum at 13 Lincoln's Inn Fields, and every student\nof the religion of the Egyptians should examine it.\n\nIV. The RITUAL OF EMBALMMENT.--Two important fragments of a copy of this\nwork are preserved in the Museum of the Louvre (No. 5158), and a part of\nanother in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo (No. 3); the former copy was\nwritten for a priest of Amen called Heru, and the latter for a priest\ncalled Hetra. These fragments of the work describe minutely the process\nof mummifying certain parts of a human body, and state what materials\nwere employed by the embalmer. Moreover, it gives the texts of the\nmagical and religious spells that were ordered to be recited by the\npriest who superintended the embalmment, the effect of which was to\n\"make divine\" each member of the body, and to secure for it the\nprotecting influence of the god or goddess who presided over it. The\nfollowing extract refers to the embalming of the head: \"Then anoint the\nhead of the deceased and all his mouth with oil, both the head and the\nface, and wrap it in the bandages of Harmakhis in Hebit. The bandage of\nthe goddess Nekhebet shall be put on the forehead, the bandage of Hathor\nin Heliopolis on the face, the bandage of Thoth on the ears, and the\nbandage of Nebt-hetepet on the back of the neck. All the coverings of\nthe head and all the strips of linen used in fastening them shall be\ntaken from sheets of linen that have been examined as to quality and\ntexture in the presence of the inspector of the mysteries. On the head\nof the deceased shall be the bandage of Sekhmet, beloved of Ptah, in two\npieces. On the two ears two bandages called the \"Complete.\" On the\nnostrils two bandages called \"Nehai\" and \"Smen.\" On the cheeks two\nbandages called \"He shall live.\" On the forehead four pieces of linen\ncalled the \"shining ones.\" On the skull two pieces called \"The two Eyes\nof Ra in their fullness.\" On the two sides of the face and ears\ntwenty-two pieces. As to the mouth two inside, and two out. On the chin\ntwo pieces. On the back of the neck four large pieces. Then tie the\nwhole head firmly with a strip of linen two fingers wide, and anoint a\nsecond time, and then fill up all the crevices with the oil already\nmentioned. Then say, \"O august goddess, Lady of the East, Mistress of\nthe West, come and enter into the two ears of Osiris. O mighty goddess,\nwho art ever young, O great one, Lady of the East, Mistress of the West,\nlet there be breathing in the head of the deceased in the Tuat. Let him\nsee with his eyes, hear with his ears, breathe with his nose, pronounce\nwith his mouth, and speak with his tongue in the Tuat. Accept his voice\nin the Hall of Truth, and let him be proved to have been a speaker of\nthe truth in the Hall of Keb, in the presence of the Great God, the Lord\nof Amenti.\""
}

  "passage_text": "V. The RITUAL OF THE DIVINE CULT.--This title is commonly given to a\nwork consisting of sixty-six chapters, which were recited daily by the\nhigh priest of Amen-Ra, the King of the Gods, in his temple at Thebes,\nduring the performance of a series of ceremonies of a highly important\nand symbolical character. The text of this Ritual is found cut in\nhieroglyphs on the walls of the temple of Seti I at Abydos, and written\nin hieratic upon papyri preserved in the Imperial Museum in Berlin. The\nwork was originally intended to be recited by the king himself daily,\nbut it was soon found that the Lord of Egypt could not spare the time\nnecessary for its recital each day, and he therefore was personified by\nthe high priest of each temple in which the Ritual was performed. The\nobject of the Ritual was to place the king in direct contact with his\ngod Amen-Ra once a day. The king was an incarnation of Amen-Ra, and\nruled Egypt as the representative upon earth of the god. He drew his\npower and wisdom direct from the god, and it was believed that these\nrequired renewal daily. To bring about this renewal of the divine spirit\nin the god's vicegerent upon earth, the king entered the temple in the\nearly morning, and performed ceremonies and recited formulæ that\npurified both the sanctuary and himself. He then advanced to the shrine,\nwhich contained a small gilded wooden figure of the god, inlaid with\nprecious stones and provided with a movable head, arms, and legs, and\nopened it and knelt down before the figure. He performed further\nceremonies of purification, and finally took the figure of the god in\nhis arms and embraced it. During this embrace the divine power of\nAmen-Ra, which was in the gilded figure at that moment, passed into the\nbody of the king, and the divine power and wisdom, which were in the\nking as the god's representative, were renewed. The king then closed the\ndoors of the shrine and left the sanctuary for a short time. When he\nreturned he opened the shrine again, and made adoration to the god, and\npresented a series of offerings that symbolised Truth. After this the\nking dressed the figure of the god in sacred apparel, and decorated it.\nThen, having performed further acts of worship before it, he closed the\ndoors of the shrine, sealed them with mud seals, and left the sanctuary.\n\nVI. The BOOK \"MAY MY NAME FLOURISH.\"--This was a very popular funerary\nwork in the Roman Period. It is a development of a long prayer that is\nfound in the Pyramid Texts, and was written by the priests and used as a\nspell to make the name of the deceased flourish eternally in heaven and\non the earth. Many copies of it, written on narrow strips of papyrus,\nare preserved in the British Museum.\n\nVII. The BOOK OF AAPEP, the great enemy of the Sun-god.--Aapep was the\ngod of evil, who became incarnate in many forms, especially in wild and\nsavage animals and in monster serpents and venomous reptiles of every\nkind. He was supposed to take the form of a huge serpent and to lie in\nwait near the portals of the dawn daily, so that he might swallow up the\nsun as he was about to rise in the eastern sky. He was accompanied by\nlegions of devils and fiends, red and black, and by all the powers of\nstorm, tempest, hurricane, whirlwind, thunder and lightning, and he was\nthe deadly foe of all order, both physical and moral, and of all good in\nheaven and in earth. At certain times during the day and night the\npriests in the temple of Amen-Ra recited a series of chapters, and\nperformed a number of magical ceremonies, which were intended to\nstrengthen the arms of the Sun-god, and give him power to overcome the\nresistance of Aapep. These chapters acted on Aapep as spells, and they\nparalysed the monster just as he was about to attack the Sun-god. The\ngod then approached and shot his fiery darts into him, and his attendant\ngods hacked the monster's body to pieces, which shrivelled up under the\nburning heat of the rays of the Sun-god, and all the devils and fiends\nof darkness fled shrieking in terror at their leader's fate. The sun\nthen rose on this world, and all the stars and spirits of the morning\nand all the gods of heaven sang for joy. The complete text of this book\nis found in a long papyrus dated in the reign of Alexander II in the\nBritish Museum (No. 10,188)."

  "passage_text": "VIII. The INSTRUCTIONS, OR PRECEPTS OF TUAUF to his son Pepi.--Two
copies of this work, which has also been called a "Hymn in praise of
learning," are contained in a papyri preserved in the British Museum
(Sallier II and Anastasi VII). These "Instructions" in reality represent
the advice of a father to his son, whom he was sending to school to be
trained for the profession of the scribe. Whether the boy was merely
sorry to leave his home, or whether he disliked the profession which his
father had chosen for him, is not clear, but from first to last the
father urges him to apply himself to the pursuit of learning, which, in
his opinion, is the foundation of all great and lasting success. He
says, "I have compared the people who are artisans and handicraftsmen
[with the scribe], and indeed I am convinced that there is nothing
superior to letters. Plunge into the study of Egyptian Learning, as thou
wouldst plunge into the river, and thou wilt find that this is so. I
would that thou wouldst love Learning as thou lovest thy mother. I wish
I were able to make thee to see how beautiful Learning is. It is more
important than any trade in the world. Learning is not a mere phrase,
for the man who devoteth himself thereto from his youth is honoured, and
he is despatched on missions. I have watched the blacksmith at the door
of his furnace. His hands are like crocodiles' hide, and he stinketh
worse than fishes' eggs. The metal worker hath no more rest than the
peasant on the farm. The stone mason--at the end of the day his arms are
powerless; he sitteth huddled up together until the morning, and his
knees and back are broken. The barber shaveth until far into the night,
he only resteth when he eateth. He goeth from one street to another
looking for work. He breaketh his arms to fill his belly, and, like the
bees, he eateth his own labour. The builder of houses doeth his work
with difficulty; he is exposed to all weathers, and he must cling to the
walls which he is building like a creeping plant. His clothes are in a
horrible state, and he washeth his body only once a day. The farmer
weareth always the same clothes. His voice is like the croak of a bird,
his skin is cracked by the wind; if he is healthy his health is that of
the beasts. If he be ill he lieth down among them, and he sleepeth on
the damp irrigated land. The envoy to foreign lands bequeatheth his
property to his children before he setteth out, being afraid that he
will be killed either by wild beasts of the desert or by the nomads
therein. When he is in Egypt, what then? No sooner hath he arrived at
home than he is sent off on another mission. As for the dyer, his
fingers stink like rotten fish, and his clothes are absolutely horrors.
The shoemaker is a miserable wretch. He is always asking for work, and
his health is that of a dying fish. The washerman is neighbour to the
crocodile. His food is mixed up with his clothes, and every member of
him is unclean. The catcher of water-fowl, even though he dive in the
Nile, may catch nothing. The trade of the fisherman is the worst of all.
He is in blind terror of the crocodile, and falleth among crocodiles."
The text continues with a few further remarks on the honourable
character of the profession of the scribe, and ends with a series of
Precepts of the same character as those found in the works of Ptah-hetep
and the scribe Ani, from which extracts have already been given.

IX. MEDICAL PAPYRI.--The Egyptians possessed a good practical knowledge
of the anatomy of certain parts of the human body, but there is no
evidence that they practised dissection before the arrival of the Greeks
in Egypt. The medical papyri that have come down to us contain a large
number of short, rough-and-ready descriptions of certain diseases, and
prescriptions of very great interest. The most important medical papyrus
known is that which was bought at Luxor by the late Professor Ebers in
1872-3, and which is now preserved in Leipzig. This papyrus is about 65
feet long, and the text is written in the hieratic character. It was
written in the ninth year of the reign of a king who is not yet
satisfactorily identified, but who probably lived before the period of
the rule of the eighteenth dynasty, perhaps about 1800 B.C. A short
papyrus in the British Museum contains extracts from it, and other
papyri with somewhat similar contents are preserved in the Museums of
Paris, Leyden, Berlin, and California.

X. MAGICAL PAPYRI.--The widespread use of magic in Egypt in all ages
suggests that the magical literature of Egypt must have been very
large. Much of it was incorporated at a very early period into the
Religious Literature of the country, and was used for legitimate
purposes, in fact for the working of what we call "white magic." The
Egyptian saw no wrong in the working of magic, and it was only condemned
by him when the magician wished to produce evil results. The gods
themselves were supposed to use spells and incantations, and every
traveller by land or water carried with him magical formulæ which he
recited when he was in danger from the wild beasts of the desert or the
crocodile of the river and its canals. Specimens of these will be found
in the famous magical papyri in the British Museum, _e.g._ the Salt
Papyrus, the Rhind Papyrus, and the Harris Papyrus. Under this heading
may be mentioned Papyrus Sallier IV in the British Museum, which
contains a list of lucky and unlucky days. Here is a specimen of its
contents:

    1st day of Hathor. The whole day is lucky. There is festival in
    heaven with Ra and Hathor.

    2nd day of Hathor. The whole day is lucky. The gods go out. The
    goddess Uatchet comes from Tep to the gods who are in the shrine of
    the bull, in order to protect the divine members.

    3rd day of Hathor. The whole day is lucky.

    4th day of Hathor. The whole day is unlucky. The house of the man
    who goes on a voyage on that day comes to ruin."
}

  "passage_text": "6th day of Hathor. The whole day is unlucky. Do not light a fire in
    thy house on this day, and do not look at one.

    18th day of Pharmuthi. The whole day is unlucky. Do not bathe on
    this day.

    day.

    22nd day of Pharmuthi. The whole day is unlucky. He who is born on
    this day will die on this day.

    23rd day of Pharmuthi. The first two-thirds of the day are unlucky,
    and the last third lucky.

XI. LEGAL DOCUMENTS.--The first legal document written in Egypt was the
will of Ra, in which he bequeathed all his property and the inheritance
of the throne of Egypt to his first-born son Horus. Tradition asserted
that this Will was preserved in the Library of the Sun-god in
Heliopolis. The inscriptions contain many allusions to the Laws of
Egypt, but no document containing any connected statement of them has
come down to us. In the great inscription of Heruemheb, the last king of
the eighteenth dynasty, a large number of good laws are given, but it
must be confessed that as a whole the administration of the Law in many
parts of Egypt must always have been very lax. Texts relating to
bequests, endowments, grants of land, &c., are very difficult to
translate, because it is well-nigh impossible to find equivalents for
Egyptian legal terms. In the British Museum are two documents in
hieratic that were drawn up in connection with prosecutions which the
Government of Egypt undertook of certain thieves who had broken into
some of the royal tombs at Thebes and robbed them, and of certain other
thieves who had robbed the royal treasury and made away with a large
amount of silver (Nos. 10,221, 10,052, 10,053, and 10,054). Equally
interesting is the roll that describes the prosecution of certain highly
placed officials and relations of Rameses III who had conspired against
him and wanted to kill him. Several of the conspirators were compelled
to commit suicide. The text is written in hieratic on papyrus, and is
preserved in the Royal Museum, Leyden.

XII. HISTORICAL ROMANCES.--Examples of these are the narrative of the
capture of the town of Joppa in Palestine by an officer of Thothmes III,
and the history of the dispute that broke out between Seqenenra, King of
Upper Egypt, and Aapepi, King of Avaris in the Delta. These are written
in hieratic and are preserved in the British Museum, in Harris Papyrus
500, and Sallier No. 1 (10,185).

XIII. MATHEMATICS.--The chief source of our knowledge of the Mathematics
of the Egyptians is the Rhind Papyrus in the British Museum (No.
10,057), which was written before 1700 B.C., probably during the reign
of one of the Hyksos kings. The papyrus contains a number of simple
arithmetical examples and several geometrical problems. The workings
out of these prove that the Egyptian spared himself no trouble in making
his calculations, and that he worked out both his arithmetical examples
and problems in the most cumbrous and laborious way possible. He never
studied mathematics in order to make progress in his knowledge of the
science, but simply for purely practical everyday work; as long as his
knowledge enabled him to obtain results which he knew from experience
were substantially correct he was content.
